title: Rina's wedding
goal: Find your way through a Javanese wedding in Jakarta, from the *seserahan* trays to the *akad*, the *sungkeman* and the *resepsi*, and give good wishes that sound right for the occasion.
bekal: name the stages of a Javanese wedding: *siraman, midodareni, akad, sungkeman, resepsi*
count gifts with the formal counters: *seperangkat alat salat, sepasang sepatu, selembar kain*
wish people well at weddings and other milestones: *Semoga menjadi keluarga yang sakinah…*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Menata seserahan
dialogs.intro: A Saturday in late October, the day before the wedding, in the house Andi's family has rented in East Jakarta for the week. Andi's mother, Bu Hartini, has come up from Solo with trays of gifts to arrange before evening, and she has recruited Sarah.

notes: **Seserahan** (from *serah*, to hand over) are the gifts the groom's family brings the bride before the wedding, as a sign that he is ready to provide for her: clothes, shoes, cosmetics, jewellery, cakes, fruit. They are carried in on decorated trays (*nampan*) by a procession of relatives. They are not the same as the *mahar* or *mas kawin*, the bride-price handed over during the *akad* itself.

**Monggo** is Javanese “please, go ahead”, and Bu Hartini, like Andi's whole family, is from Solo. Javanese families in Jakarta slip into Javanese words at home and especially at weddings. Her *pinter* (standard *pintar*, clever) is the Javanese-flavoured pronunciation, warm and a little motherly.

**Seperangkat alat salat** — a complete set of prayer things: *mukena* (the white prayer robe worn by women), *sajadah* (prayer mat) and often a Qur'an. It is also the commonest *mahar*, and every Indonesian knows the groom's line at the *akad*: *…dengan mas kawin seperangkat alat salat dibayar tunai* — “…with a set of prayer things as the bride-price, paid in full”.

**Sidomukti** is one of the classic wedding batik patterns of Solo and Yogya. *Sido* is Javanese for “to become, to last”, and *mukti* means noble and prosperous. Many batik patterns carry a wish like this, and older relatives will happily explain them if you ask *Motifnya artinya apa?*

**Rezeki berlapis-lapis.** *Rezeki* (from Arabic) is fortune, livelihood, the good things God provides. *Berlapis-lapis* (in many layers) is a play on *lapis legit*, the rich Dutch-Indonesian layer cake. Wedding gifts are full of puns like this.
**Nyicip, makanya.** *Nyicip* is the spoken form of *mencicipi*, to have a taste. *Makanya* (that's why, which is why) opens a conclusion, often with a hint of “I told you so”.

grammars.title: A Javanese wedding, step by step
body: Customs vary by region and by family, but a Muslim Javanese wedding in Jakarta usually follows this order over two or three days.

head: Event
When
What happens
rows: the formal proposal between the families (A2 Unit 20)
the bride and groom are bathed with flower water by their elders
the bride's last night as a maiden; the *seserahan* arrive
the Islamic marriage contract, *ijab kabul*, before a registrar
the couple kneel before their parents and ask forgiveness and blessing
the reception: guests, food, photos on the *pelaminan*
a second reception held by the groom's family

after: *Ngunduh mantu* is Javanese for “harvesting the son- or daughter-in-law”. Andi's family will hold theirs in Solo, so Rina gets two receptions and Sarah may get invited to both.
The *akad* is small and family-only; the *resepsi* is where the hundreds of guests come. An invitation will tell you which one you are invited to.

grammars.title: Counting gifts: se- + counter
body: In everyday speech you can say *satu* with almost anything. In a list of gifts, a *mahar*, a menu or a formal letter, Indonesian uses *se-* (one) plus a counter that describes the thing's shape.

head: Counter
Used for
Example
rows: *selembar kain batik, selembar uang seratus ribu*

after: For two or more, replace *se-* with the number: *dua pasang sepatu*, *tiga lembar kain*, *lima orang tamu*.
⚠️ *Satu set* is fine in speech, as Bu Hartini says; *seperangkat* is what goes on the card that labels the tray.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Di pelaminan
dialogs.intro: Sunday evening, at the reception hall. Sarah has just given her short speech as Rina's best friend. Now she joins the long queue of guests going up to the *pelaminan*, the decorated dais where the couple sit and receive everyone.

notes: **Tahu nggak?** At the end of a sentence it means “you know what?”, “did you know?”, and it is pure enthusiasm, not a real question. Rina's *Mama* is what many middle-class Jakartans call their mother; others say *Ibu*, *Bunda* or *Mami*.

**Paes and sanggul.** *Paes* is the black, scalloped forehead make-up of a Javanese bride, drawn freehand by a specialist, the *perias*. The *sanggul* is the bun, often with fresh jasmine and a real weight to it. In the Solo style, Andi wears a *beskap* jacket and a *blangkon* headcloth to match.

**Selamat menempuh hidup baru** — “congratulations on starting a new life” — is the standard wedding greeting, printed on every card. *Selamat berbahagia* (be happy) is a shorter alternative. Muslim friends may also say the Arabic *Barakallahu lakuma* (God bless you both).

**Sakinah, mawadah, warahmah** (Arabic: peaceful, loving, merciful) is the classic Muslim wedding wish, from the Qur'an. You will also see it spelled *mawaddah* and shortened to *SAMAWA* in messages. It is fine for a non-Muslim friend to say it to a Muslim couple, and they will be pleased.

**Momongan** (Javanese: a baby to carry) is a gentle word for a child you hope to have. Wishing a new couple *momongan* is normal and kind at a wedding. ⚠️ Asking a couple *Kapan punya anak?* a year later is a different matter: many find it intrusive.

**Prasmanan** is a buffet. At most receptions guests first sign the guest book (*buku tamu*) and drop their gift envelope (*amplop*) into a box, then queue to shake hands on the *pelaminan*, and eat standing or at small tables. Nobody expects you to stay long.

grammars.title: Wishing well with semoga
body: *Semoga* (may, let's hope) is followed by an ordinary sentence, often with a passive verb because God or fate is the unspoken doer. The polite answer to any wish is *Amin* (often written *Aamiin*) or *Terima kasih, doanya*.

head: Wish
English
When
rows: May you soon be given a child.
before an event, a trip, a birth

after: *Moga-moga* is the chattier version, and *mudah-mudahan* means the same thing and is just as common. In chat people write *smg* or *semoga ya* with an emoji of folded hands.

⚠️ *Selamat* congratulates on something that has happened (*Selamat ulang tahun*, *Selamat atas kelulusannya*); *semoga* wishes for something still to come. A wedding card usually has both: *Selamat menempuh hidup baru. Semoga bahagia selalu.*

blocks.text: A Javanese wedding is a festival of symbols, and guests are expected to recognise at least the main ones. These are the words you will hear in the MC's commentary.

where the couple sit and receive guests
the couple throw them at each other: love at first sight
the groom breaks it; the bride washes his foot

blocks.text: One idiom worth knowing: *Janur kuning belum melengkung* — “the yellow coconut leaf hasn't been bent yet” — meaning “they're not married yet, so there's still a chance”. It is said, half joking, about someone else's girlfriend or boyfriend.

sections.title: The right words for the occasion

blocks.text: Most life events have a fixed greeting that people use in person, on cards and in the family WhatsApp group. Use the formula first; add something personal after it.

head: Occasion
Indonesian
English
rows: *Semoga sukses di tempat kerja yang baru!*
Good luck in your new job!

blocks.text: Muslim friends often add *Innalillahi wa inna ilaihi raji'un* when they hear of a death, and *Alhamdulillah* when they hear of a birth. You are not expected to say these yourself, but you should recognise them.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
